title: The Evolution of Glass-Making Through the Ages
context:
A. Archaeological evidence suggests that humanity's relationship with artificial glass began around the third millennium BCE in Mesopotamia and Egypt. Prior to synthetic vitreous materials, prehistoric artisans utilized obsidian, a naturally occurring volcanic glass, to fashion razor-sharp cutting tools. Early manufactured glass, however, was neither transparent nor easily manipulated. Craftsmen combined crushed quartz or silica sand with an alkaline flux—frequently natron or plant ash—to lower melting temperatures. Using a laborious technique known as core-forming, artisans shaped molten paste around a removable clay core, creating small beads, amulets, and rudimentary perfume flasks primarily reserved for ruling elites.

B. The pivotal technological breakthrough in glass production occurred during the first century BCE along the Syro-Palestinian coast with the invention of glassblowing. By gathering a gob of molten glass on the tip of a hollow iron blowpipe and inflating it, artisans could produce vessels of unprecedented thinness and varied geometry in a fraction of the time required by core-forming. This innovation spread rapidly across the Roman Empire, democratizing what had previously been an exclusive luxury. The Romans also pioneered the architectural application of glass, casting thick panes to create the earliest known glazed windows, which transformed residential lighting and bathhouse insulation.

C. Following the decline of the Western Roman Empire, the locus of glassmaking expertise shifted eastward to the Islamic world. Between the eighth and fourteenth centuries, Islamic glassworkers refined decorative methodologies, mastering techniques such as relief cutting, luster painting, and vibrant enamelling. Cities like Damascus and Aleppo became celebrated centers for producing ornate mosque lamps and gilded beakers. Furthermore, Islamic scholars advanced chemical treatises that systematically documented flux purifications and metal oxide colorants, safeguarding and refining glass formulas that would subsequently influence European revivals.

D. By the late Middle Ages, the epicenter of fine glass production relocated to Venice. To mitigate catastrophic fire risks and safeguard industrial secrets, the Venetian Republic decreed in 1291 that all furnaces be relocated to the island of Murano. There, artisan Angelo Barovier formulated cristallo, an astonishingly clear, colorless glass achieved by treating plant ashes with manganese dioxide to neutralize iron impurities. Venice established a virtual European monopoly, implementing draconian laws that prohibited glassmakers from emigrating under penalty of treason, although skilled defectors gradually seeded Venetian techniques throughout northern Europe.

E. The seventeenth century initiated a scientific transformation in glass chemistry. In England, George Ravenscroft patented lead crystal in 1674 by introducing lead oxide into the batch, yielding a denser, highly refractive glass ideal for intricate wheel cutting. As the Industrial Revolution gained momentum, manufacturing shifted from artisanal workshops to mechanized factories. The nineteenth century witnessed the invention of the cylinder process for broad window glass, followed in 1903 by Michael Owens’ automated bottle machine, which could churn out thousands of identical containers per hour, fundamentally altering the packaging industry.

F. The mid-twentieth century brought the definitive innovation of modern flat glass: the float glass process. Developed in the 1950s by Sir Alastair Pilkington, this method involved pouring molten glass across a bath of molten tin, allowing gravity and surface tension to form perfectly flat, distortion-free sheets without mechanical grinding. Today, the float process supplies the vast majority of architectural and automotive glazing. Contemporary glass technology continues to evolve, extending beyond utilitarian containers to specialized engineered materials, including ultra-thin chemically strengthened glass for touchscreens and low-loss silica optical fibers underpinning global telecommunications.

title: Farming on Volcanic Ground
context:
A. Volcanic landscapes can appear harsh, yet many support productive farms. Their soils begin with ash, lava fragments, and other material released during eruptions. Weathering gradually breaks these materials into smaller particles and releases mineral nutrients. The resulting soil is not uniformly fertile: its properties depend on the volcano's composition, the age of its deposits, and local climate. Farmers therefore cannot assume that any field near a volcano will provide the same conditions for crops.

B. Fresh volcanic deposits may initially offer little support for cultivation. They can be coarse, unstable, and short of organic matter, while rain may wash away fine particles before plants become established. Over time, weathering and the accumulation of decaying vegetation change this picture. In humid regions, warm temperatures and frequent rainfall can speed chemical breakdown, but they may also leach soluble nutrients from the ground. The gradual development of a stable, biologically active soil often matters more to agriculture than the mere presence of volcanic minerals.

C. One advantage of many volcanic soils is their ability to retain water. Some contain abundant fine particles and weathered minerals that create small pores, allowing moisture to remain available between rain showers. This can help crops through brief dry spells. Yet water retention varies considerably: soils dominated by coarse ash or gravel may drain rapidly, leaving roots thirsty. Their structure also affects aeration, since poorly drained layers can restrict oxygen around roots. Farmers assess texture and drainage rather than treating volcanic origin as a guarantee of reliable moisture.

D. Volcanic materials may supply elements such as potassium, calcium, and magnesium, which plants use in growth. However, a high total mineral content does not necessarily mean that nutrients are immediately accessible. In some soils, phosphorus becomes bound to reactive iron and aluminium compounds, so crops cannot readily absorb it. Soil acidity can further influence nutrient availability. Testing helps farmers identify such constraints and choose suitable amendments, including organic matter or lime where appropriate. Applying fertilizer without diagnosing the underlying problem may waste money and can contribute to pollution.

E. The physical structure of volcanic soil can also benefit cultivation. Weathered ash may form aggregates that are porous enough for roots to penetrate while remaining resistant to rapid erosion. Organic matter from crop residues and animal manure improves aggregation and supports soil organisms. Nevertheless, steep volcanic slopes are vulnerable to runoff, especially after vegetation has been cleared. Terraces, contour planting, and protective ground cover slow water moving downhill and reduce the loss of fertile topsoil. These measures are particularly important where intense rain follows a dry season.

F. Agriculture on volcanic land thus depends on management as much as on geology. Farmers may select crops suited to local acidity and rainfall, maintain organic residues, and monitor nutrient levels over time. Coffee, vegetables, and fruit are grown in some volcanic regions, but no single crop thrives everywhere. Changing rainfall patterns can intensify erosion or create longer dry intervals, making water conservation and soil cover increasingly valuable. Volcanic soils offer real opportunities, but their benefits are conditional: careful observation and locally adapted practices turn geological materials into dependable farmland.

title: Pediatric Screen Engagement and Developmental Trajectories
context:
A. In recent decades, pediatric digital engagement has experienced a paradigm shift, transitioning from communal, stationary television viewing to pervasive interaction with handheld digital devices. Modern infants and young children encounter touchscreens during critical windows of neurodevelopment, when synaptic plasticity is remarkably elevated. While proponents argue that intuitive interfaces foster digital literacy, developmental specialists caution that excessive exposure during infancy can profoundly alter the trajectories of structural brain maturation. The sensory richness of portable screens often captivates young minds through rapid auditory and visual shifts, creating an artificial stimulus landscape that natural environments cannot replicate.

B. A central theoretical framework examining these effects is the displacement hypothesis, which posits that screen time harms development primarily by supplanting essential real-world activities. Time allocated to digital media inevitably curtails opportunities for unstructured tactile play, physical locomotion, and reciprocal vocal exchanges with primary caregivers. Observational studies demonstrate that when toddlers use portable tablets, their conversational turns with parents decline sharply. Because language acquisition relies heavily on dynamic, contingent verbal interactions, prolonged digital absorption during formative years is consistently correlated with expressive vocabulary deficits and communicative delays.

C. Beyond linguistic setbacks, screen immersion exerts quantifiable physiological tolls on pediatric biological rhythms. Handheld displays emit short-wavelength blue light, which directly stimulates retinal ganglion cells and subsequently inhibits the pineal gland's secretion of melatonin. In young subjects, whose ocular lenses are clearer and pupils larger than those of adults, this photochemical vulnerability is particularly acute. The resultant suppression of evening melatonin disrupts natural circadian cycles, precipitating prolonged sleep latency, frequent nocturnal awakenings, and compromised sleep architecture, which ultimately hampers memory consolidation and somatic growth.

D. Nevertheless, researchers emphasize that the developmental consequences of screen exposure are contingent upon media typology. A critical distinction is made between passive video consumption and interactive educational software embedded with cognitive scaffolding. When programs feature responsive feedback, age-appropriate narratives, and joint-attention prompts, older preschoolers can acquire early numeracy skills and domain-specific knowledge. Conversely, media saturated with rapid pacing and sensory overstimulation often overwhelms immature working memory, impeding information processing rather than facilitating intellectual advancement.

E. Emotional and behavioral self-regulation constitutes another vulnerability domain. In contemporary parenting, handheld electronics are frequently deployed as digital pacifiers to soothe distressed infants or avert public tantrums. While offering immediate behavioral compliance, this coping strategy denies children crucial opportunities to practice internal distress tolerance and emotional modulation. Longitudinal research indicates that relying on screens for affective regulation correlates with diminished executive functioning, lower frustration tolerance, and an inability to master delay of gratification during early primary school.

F. To mitigate these risks, pediatric authorities advocate for nuanced parental mediation rather than punitive total bans. Active co-viewing, wherein adults scaffold digital experiences by discussing plot elements and drawing real-world parallels, substantially buffers against negative developmental outcomes. Furthermore, establishing consistent digital hygiene—such as designating screen-free zones, enforcing tech-free meals, and curating high-quality interactive content—cultivates an intentional media environment. Through collaborative engagement and clear structural boundaries, caregivers can preserve the developmental integrity of early childhood while safely navigating digital technology.

title: Why Humans Laugh
context:
A. Laughter is often treated as a simple reaction to jokes, but researchers describe it as a complex social signal involving the brain, body and surrounding group. It can occur without deliberate humour: people laugh while greeting friends, easing tension or showing agreement. In many conversations, laughter appears more frequently during pauses than at the punchline of a joke. This suggests that its role is not merely to express amusement; it also helps people coordinate interaction. Because laughter is audible and contagious, it can communicate a person's attitude even when the words themselves are ambiguous.

B. The physical process begins with activity in several brain systems rather than one isolated “laughter centre”. Areas involved in emotion help produce the feeling of amusement, while motor regions organise the movements of the face, chest and breathing muscles. The sound is generated by repeated bursts of air pushed through the vocal tract. Unlike ordinary speech, laughter tends to follow a rhythmic pattern, with each burst occurring roughly every two-tenths of a second. This regularity may help explain why listeners can recognise laughter across different languages, even when they cannot understand the speaker's words.

C. Social context strongly influences when laughter occurs. Experiments have found that people laugh more often when they are with others than when they watch the same humorous material alone. The presence of an audience does not simply make jokes funnier; it changes how people manage affiliation and attention. In a group, laughter can signal that a comment is friendly rather than hostile, or invite others to join a shared response. Researchers also distinguish spontaneous laughter from laughter produced intentionally. The latter is usually easier to control, but listeners may detect subtle differences in timing and sound that reveal whether it is genuine.

D. One explanation for laughter's contagious quality is that hearing it activates neural systems associated with preparing a response. This does not mean that a listener must laugh, but it may lower the threshold for doing so. The effect is especially noticeable in groups, where one person's laughter can prompt another's and create a feedback loop. Shared laughter may also support social bonds by making interaction feel safer and more cooperative. However, it is not universally positive: people can laugh to exclude someone, mask discomfort or reinforce a group's boundaries. Its meaning therefore depends on who is laughing, who is listening and what has happened immediately beforehand.

E. Scientists have also investigated possible health effects. Laughter temporarily changes breathing, heart rate and muscle activity, and some studies report short-lived reductions in stress-related measures after humorous experiences. Yet these findings do not establish laughter as a treatment for illness. Samples are often small, and researchers cannot easily separate the effects of laughter from those of social contact, expectation or a pleasant activity. Claims that laughter reliably strengthens immunity or produces lasting medical benefits should therefore be treated cautiously. A more defensible conclusion is that enjoyable shared experiences can contribute to well-being, while the precise biological pathways remain under investigation.

F. Studying laughter presents practical challenges because it is spontaneous and varies between individuals and cultures. A recording made in a laboratory may not capture the same behaviour as laughter during an everyday conversation. Researchers combine methods such as acoustic analysis, observation and brain imaging, but each reveals only part of the process. Future work may compare laughter across settings and examine how listeners interpret it without relying on words. Such research could clarify why a sound that appears effortless can perform several jobs at once: expressing emotion, regulating conversation and negotiating relationships. The science of laughter is consequently not just a study of humour, but also an inquiry into how people live together.

title: Iron Arteries: How Railways Reshaped the Urban Landscape
topic: railways and the growth of cities
context:
A. The advent of steam locomotives in the early nineteenth century fundamentally altered the relationship between human settlements and physical geography. Prior to the spread of iron rails, urban growth was strictly constrained by walking distances and watercourses, creating dense, highly compact settlements with limited physical footprints. The deployment of mechanized rail transport dismantled these traditional spatial thresholds. By drastically lowering overland haulage expenses and transit intervals, railways allowed metropolitan centers to draw sustenance, raw commodities, and labor from vast hinterlands, precipitating an unprecedented era of rapid demographic expansion and spatial reorganization.

B. Within urban cores, the physical arrival of railways triggered seismic architectural and social upheavals. Because terminal stations required vast swathes of prime urban land, railway syndicates frequently demolished crowded working-class neighborhoods, termed rookeries, through compulsory purchase orders. The displaced residents were typically pushed into denser slums deeper in the municipal fabric, intensifying overcrowding. Meanwhile, the grand terminus stations themselves—often designed with palatial facades and sweeping iron-framed sheds—became civic symbols that conferred significant prestige upon their host municipalities, effectively redefining downtown commercial districts into bustling hubs of trade.

C. Concurrently, the outward expansion of tracks laid the foundation for modern suburbanization. The passage of regulatory statutes, such as the Cheap Trains Act, mandated affordable passenger services, enabling clerks and artisans to reside beyond polluted inner zones for the first time. Linear developments, known as ribbon settlements, sprouted along radial railway corridors, eventually fusing into expansive metropolitan belts. This geographic dispersion fostered acute socio-economic sorting, as leafy peripheral communities were marketed exclusively to the burgeoning middle tier of society, cementing distinct suburban class profiles that endured for generations.

D. Industrial geography underwent an equally dramatic restructuring as factories adapted to the new transport paradigm. Previously tied to coastal docks or inland canals, heavy manufacturing progressively clustered alongside extensive marshalling yards and dedicated private sidings. The reliable delivery of bulk fuel, particularly anthracite and bituminous coal, severed factories from geographic energy constraints. Furthermore, urban rail depots transformed wholesale distribution, allowing perishable provisions like fluid milk and seasonal produce to arrive daily without spoilage, which significantly bolstered public health in expanding industrial towns by providing fresher nourishment.

E. On a national scale, the rail grid established a definitive urban hierarchy across formerly isolated regions. Towns designated as junction points or railway workshops, such as Swindon or Crewe, mutated from sleepy agrarian villages into sprawling specialized centers dominated by mechanical engineering. Conversely, historical market settlements that resisted rail connections or were bypassed by surveyor plans suffered swift economic marginalization. Moreover, the imperative of coordinating complex train movements necessitated the adoption of standardized railway time, an innovation that systematically eradicated idiosyncratic local solar calculations across all regional territories.

F. In the contemporary era, the enduring legacy of railway-led urbanism continues to evolve through sustainable transit-oriented development. Planners increasingly prioritize high-density residential and commercial clusters around transit hubs to curb highway congestion and carbon output. Concurrently, obsolete rail infrastructure, including disused viaducts and abandoned goods yards, has provided prime brownfield sites for ambitious urban regeneration projects. Far from being a declining artifact of the Industrial Revolution, the railway corridor remains a potent organizing axis for twenty-first-century metropolitan growth and ecological renewal.

questions.quote: Towns designated as junction points or railway workshops, such as Swindon or Crewe, mutated from sleepy agrarian villages

questions.prompt: Market towns experienced rapid ____ if they were ignored by rail planners or opposed train connections.
questions.why: Đoạn E chỉ rõ những thị trấn chợ truyền thống từ chối hoặc bị tuyến đường sắt bỏ qua đã phải chịu cảnh bị gạt ra ngoài lề kinh tế nhanh chóng ('economic marginalization').
questions.quote: historical market settlements that resisted rail connections or were bypassed by surveyor plans suffered swift economic marginalization.

questions.prompt: The need to align train schedules led to the introduction of ____.
questions.why: Đoạn E nêu rõ yêu cầu điều phối lịch trình tàu hỏa đã dẫn đến việc áp dụng giờ đường sắt chuẩn hóa ('standardized railway time').
questions.quote: necessitated the adoption of standardized railway time, an innovation that systematically eradicated idiosyncratic local solar calculations

questions.prompt: Concentrating homes and businesses near transport stations is intended to decrease carbon emissions and ____.
questions.why: Đoạn F giải thích việc quy hoạch khu dân cư và thương mại mật độ cao quanh các đầu mối giao thông nhằm kiềm chế khí thải carbon và nạn tắc đường cao tốc ('highway congestion').
questions.quote: clusters around transit hubs to curb highway congestion and carbon output.

questions.prompt: Outdated railway properties are now frequently utilized as ____ for city renewal schemes.
questions.why: Đoạn F chỉ ra rằng cơ sở hạ tầng đường sắt cũ kỹ, bỏ hoang hiện cung cấp các khu đất công nghiệp cũ đắc địa ('prime brownfield sites') cho các dự án tái thiết đô thị.
questions.quote: obsolete rail infrastructure, including disused viaducts and abandoned goods yards, has provided prime brownfield sites for ambitious urban regeneration projects.

title: Deciphering the Language of Honeybees
context:
A. The complex social structure of the Western honeybee (Apis mellifera) relies on intricate communication mechanisms that coordinate thousands of individual workers. The initial breakthrough in deciphering this communication occurred through the mid-twentieth-century work of Austrian ethologist Karl von Frisch. Von Frisch established that returning foragers perform distinct movements on the vertical wax combs. For nectar sources located within approximately fifty metres, bees execute a simple "round dance," which alerts nestmates to floral abundance nearby without specifying direction. Beyond this threshold, however, foragers transition to the far more sophisticated "waggle dance," an encoded message that translates spatial coordinates into sensory cues accessible in the dark hive.

B. The waggle dance operates as a vector communication system conveying both distance and direction. During the dance, a forager runs forward in a straight line while vigorously vibrating her abdomen, then circles back to alternate sides. The orientation of this straight run relative to vertical gravity precisely mirrors the flight angle required relative to the current solar azimuth. Furthermore, the duration of the waggle phase correlates with distance: roughly one second of wagging corresponds to one kilometre of flight. In conjunction with abdominal movements, the dancer produces low-frequency acoustic vibrations and air currents generated by thoracic muscles, which surrounding followers detect through their antennae and specialised subgenual organs.

C. Visual and vibrational cues are complemented by a pervasive chemical vocabulary. Pheromones secreted from exocrine glands govern long-term colony cohesion and immediate behavioural shifts. For example, the queen releases queen mandibular pheromone, a complex chemical blend that suppresses worker ovary development and maintains communal stability. When facing acute danger, defender bees release alarm pheromones from their sting apparatus, primarily consisting of isopentyl acetate. This pungent compound instantly recruits aggressive defenders to neutralize threats. Similarly, foraging bees deposit secretions from the Nasonov gland at rich nectar patches or nest entrances, guiding disoriented nestmates toward critical targets.

D. Beyond recruitment, honeybees employ inhibitory signals to regulate collective labour. One prominent mechanism is the "stop signal," during which a worker delivers brief head-butts accompanied by short acoustic pulses to an active dancer. This signal is triggered when the scout encounters hazards, such as aggressive predators or severe resource depletion, effectively damping recruitment to perilous sites. Another modulating behaviour is the "tremble dance," performed by foragers returning with rich nectar when receiver bees are overwhelmed, prompting more workers to shift into nectar-processing duties rather than foraging.

E. During reproductive swarming, communication culminates in collective consensus building. When an established colony reproduces, several thousand bees leave with the old queen and cluster temporarily on a nearby tree branch. Hundreds of veteran scouts search the surrounding landscape for prospective nesting cavities, assessing factors such as entrance size, cavity volume, and height above ground. Returning scouts perform waggle dances to advertise potential sites, with dance intensity reflecting cavity quality. Over several days, a phenomenon known as quorum sensing occurs: once a critical threshold of scouts congregates at a single superior location, the entire swarm takes flight toward its new home.

F. Contemporary neuroethological research continues to reveal further layers of subtlety, including the use of biomimetic robotic bees to manipulate recruitment. However, this sophisticated communication network is increasingly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances. Sublethal exposure to neonicotinoid pesticides impairs associative learning, weakens spatial memory, and distorts the precision of distance encoding during waggle runs. Additionally, atmospheric pollution alters floral scent plumes, hindering olfactory communication between plants and foragers. Preserving these evolutionary marvels requires a concerted effort to mitigate ecological stressors that disrupt bee dialogue.

questions.prompt: Karl von Frisch discovered that returning worker bees carry out specific movements upon the hive's ____.
questions.why: Đoạn A nêu rõ Karl von Frisch đã phát hiện ra rằng ong thợ trở về tổ thực hiện các chuyển động riêng biệt trên các bánh tổ sáp dựng đứng ('vertical wax combs').
questions.quote: Von Frisch established that returning foragers perform distinct movements on the vertical wax combs.

questions.prompt: Bees perform a round dance when food is situated within around ____ of the nest.
questions.why: Đoạn A giải thích rằng khi nguồn mật ở trong phạm vi khoảng 50 mét ('approximately fifty metres'), ong sẽ thực hiện điệu múa tròn đơn giản.
questions.quote: For nectar sources located within approximately fifty metres, bees execute a simple "round dance," which alerts nestmates to floral abundance nearby without specifying direction.

questions.prompt: The round dance informs other bees about food availability nearby but provides no details about its ____.
questions.why: Đoạn A chỉ ra rằng điệu múa tròn chỉ thông báo cho ong cùng tổ biết hoa nở rộ ở gần mà không nêu rõ phương hướng ('without specifying direction').
questions.quote: which alerts nestmates to floral abundance nearby without specifying direction.

questions.prompt: Foragers switch to the more complex ____ once food resources are located further away.
questions.why: Đoạn A chỉ ra rằng khi vượt quá mốc 50 mét, ong chuyển sang hình thức múa lắc đuôi tinh vi hơn ('waggle dance').
questions.quote: Beyond this threshold, however, foragers transition to the far more sophisticated "waggle dance," an encoded message that translates spatial coordinates into sensory cues accessible in the dark hive.

questions.prompt: During the straight run of the waggle dance, a worker bee intensely vibrates her ____.
questions.why: Đoạn B mô tả rằng trong khi múa đoạn đường thẳng, ong thợ rung mạnh phần bụng ('abdomen') của mình.
questions.quote: During the dance, a forager runs forward in a straight line while vigorously vibrating her abdomen, then circles back to alternate sides.

questions.prompt: The angle of the bee's straight run against gravity reflects the flight path in relation to the ____.
questions.why: Đoạn B khẳng định hướng của đường chạy thẳng so với trọng lực phản ánh chính xác góc bay so với góc phương vị mặt trời ('solar azimuth' hoặc 'current solar azimuth').
questions.quote: The orientation of this straight run relative to vertical gravity precisely mirrors the flight angle required relative to the current solar azimuth.

questions.prompt: Each second spent wagging in the dance represents approximately ____ of travel distance.
questions.why: Đoạn B nêu rõ thời lượng của pha lắc đuôi tương quan với khoảng cách: khoảng một giây lắc đuôi ứng với một kilômét bay ('one kilometre of flight').
questions.quote: roughly one second of wagging corresponds to one kilometre of flight.

questions.prompt: Bees observing the dancer pick up vibrations using both their antennae and their ____.
questions.why: Đoạn B đề cập những con ong xung quanh cảm nhận rung động âm thanh qua râu và các cơ quan dưới gối chuyên biệt ('specialised subgenual organs').
questions.quote: which surrounding followers detect through their antennae and specialised subgenual organs.

questions.prompt: Chemical signals that maintain colony unity are produced by the bees' ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C nêu rằng pheromone tiết ra từ các tuyến ngoại tiết ('exocrine glands') duy trì sự gắn kết lâu dài của cả bầy ong.
questions.quote: Pheromones secreted from exocrine glands govern long-term colony cohesion and immediate behavioural shifts.

questions.prompt: The queen produces a substance that prevents the development of worker bees' ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C giải thích ong chúa tiết ra pheromone tuyến hàm nhằm ức chế sự phát triển buồng trứng của ong thợ ('suppresses worker ovary development').
questions.quote: the queen releases queen mandibular pheromone, a complex chemical blend that suppresses worker ovary development and maintains communal stability.

questions.prompt: The alarm substance emitted by defender bees mainly consists of ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C chỉ ra khi có nguy hiểm, ong bảo vệ tiết pheromone báo động chứa thành phần chủ yếu là 'isopentyl acetate'.
questions.quote: When facing acute danger, defender bees release alarm pheromones from their sting apparatus, primarily consisting of isopentyl acetate.

questions.prompt: Foragers mark productive feeding areas and hive doorways with secretions from the ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C cho biết ong đi lấy mật tiết dịch từ tuyến Nasonov ('Nasonov gland') tại các thảm hoa dồi dào hoặc lối vào tổ.
questions.quote: Similarly, foraging bees deposit secretions from the Nasonov gland at rich nectar patches or nest entrances, guiding disoriented nestmates toward critical targets.

questions.prompt: Workers transmit a stop signal by combining short pulses of sound with ____ to an active dancer.
questions.why: Đoạn D mô tả rằng khi đưa ra tín hiệu dừng, ong thợ thực hiện những cú húc đầu ngắn ('brief head-butts') kèm các xung âm thanh ngắn.
questions.quote: One prominent mechanism is the "stop signal," during which a worker delivers brief head-butts accompanied by short acoustic pulses to an active dancer.

questions.prompt: A stop signal may be provoked if scouts come across threats like resource loss or ____.
questions.why: Đoạn D giải thích tín hiệu dừng bị kích hoạt khi ong thám sát gặp kẻ săn mồi hung dữ ('aggressive predators') hoặc cạn kiệt tài nguyên.
questions.quote: This signal is triggered when the scout encounters hazards, such as aggressive predators or severe resource depletion, effectively damping recruitment to perilous sites.

questions.prompt: Bees perform a tremble dance when individuals responsible for receiving nectar are ____.
questions.why: Đoạn D nói rõ điệu múa run rẩy ('tremble dance') diễn ra khi số ong tiếp nhận mật hoa bị quá tải ('overwhelmed').
questions.quote: performed by foragers returning with rich nectar when receiver bees are overwhelmed, prompting more workers to shift into nectar-processing duties

questions.prompt: During swarming, thousands of bees depart alongside the ____ before finding a permanent home.
questions.why: Đoạn E giải thích rằng khi đàn ong phân đàn sinh sản, hàng ngàn con ong sẽ rời tổ cùng con ong chúa cũ ('old queen').
questions.quote: When an established colony reproduces, several thousand bees leave with the old queen and cluster temporarily on a nearby tree branch.

questions.prompt: The vigour of a scout bee's dance corresponds to the ____ of the proposed nest site.
questions.why: Đoạn E khẳng định cường độ múa lắc đuôi của ong thám sát thể hiện chất lượng khoang tổ ('cavity quality') tiềm năng.
questions.quote: Returning scouts perform waggle dances to advertise potential sites, with dance intensity reflecting cavity quality.

questions.prompt: Swarm relocation is decided through a collective process termed ____.
questions.why: Đoạn E làm rõ hiện tượng đạt đồng thuận tập thể để chuyển đàn đến nơi ở mới được gọi là cảm nhận số đông ('quorum sensing').
questions.quote: Over several days, a phenomenon known as quorum sensing occurs: once a critical threshold of scouts congregates at a single superior location

questions.prompt: Contact with neonicotinoid pesticides can damage bees' ____ and associative learning.
questions.why: Đoạn F cho biết việc phơi nhiễm thuốc trừ sâu neonicotinoid gây suy giảm học liên kết và làm suy yếu trí nhớ không gian ('spatial memory').
questions.quote: Sublethal exposure to neonicotinoid pesticides impairs associative learning, weakens spatial memory, and distorts the precision of distance encoding during waggle runs.

questions.prompt: Odour-based communication is disrupted when atmospheric pollution modifies ____.
questions.why: Đoạn F nêu rõ ô nhiễm khí quyển làm biến đổi các luồng mùi hương hoa ('floral scent plumes'), gây khó khăn cho việc giao tiếp bằng mùi.
questions.quote: Additionally, atmospheric pollution alters floral scent plumes, hindering olfactory communication between plants and foragers.
